title: Chemistry
summary: Matter and atomic structure, the periodic table and element records, acids-bases-pH and common compound names, ores and alloys, carbon compounds, fuels, polymers, industrial processes and pollution. CGL asks 1-2 direct factual questions.

subtopics.title: Matter, separation methods and atomic structure
subtopics.concept: Matter is anything with mass that takes up space. This lesson covers its states, how to separate mixtures, and what an atom is made of. It ends with the mole and two gas laws. Most questions are fact recall, plus one or two small calculations.

tricks.title: Iso-words by the letter
tricks.body: Isotopes share the atomic number (P for protons). Isobars share A, the mass number. Isotones share neutrons.

example.q: Deuterium and tritium are what to each other?
steps: Both are hydrogen, so atomic number is 1.
Mass numbers differ: 2 and 3.

tricks.title: Sublimation list: CNIAD
tricks.body: Camphor, Naphthalene, Iodine, Ammonium chloride, Dry ice. If an option is on this list, it sublimes.

mistakes.wrong: Calling milk a true solution.
mistakes.right: Milk is a colloid (an emulsion). It scatters light.

mistakes.wrong: Saying tritium is stable.
mistakes.right: Tritium is the radioactive isotope of hydrogen.

mistakes.wrong: Treating rusting or curdling as a physical change.
mistakes.right: Both make new substances, so both are chemical changes.

mistakes.wrong: Using Celsius in Charles's law.
mistakes.right: Add 273 to get kelvin before you divide.

mistakes.wrong: Using distillation for petroleum.
mistakes.right: Its parts boil close together. Use fractional distillation.

subtopics.notes:
### States of matter
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. It has five states.

- **Solid, liquid and gas** are the three everyday states.
- **Plasma** is the fourth state. It is ionised gas, found in the Sun, stars, lightning and neon signs.
- **Bose-Einstein condensate** is the fifth state. Matter is cooled almost to absolute zero. S.N. Bose and Einstein predicted it.

**Sublimation** is a solid turning straight into vapour. Five substances are the exam favourites: camphor, naphthalene balls, iodine, ammonium chloride and dry ice (solid CO₂).

### Physical and chemical change
A **physical change** alters only the form. It is reversible, and no new substance forms. Melting ice and dissolving sugar are examples.

A **chemical change** makes a new substance. Burning, rusting, curdling of milk, cooking and digestion are examples.

> **Tip:** Ask one question: is a new substance made? Yes means chemical. No means physical.

### Separating mixtures
A mixture keeps the properties of its parts. Match the method to the job.

| Method | Use |
|---|---|
| Chromatography | Dyes in ink, pigments, drugs in blood |
| Distillation | Liquids with very different boiling points; pure water |
| Fractional distillation | Petroleum parts, liquefied air |
| Centrifugation | Cream from milk, blood tests |
| Sublimation | Salt mixed with camphor or ammonium chloride |
| Crystallisation | Pure salt or copper sulphate from a solution |
| Separating funnel | Immiscible liquids such as oil and water |
| Filtration, evaporation, magnet | Insoluble solid, dissolved solid, iron filings from sand |

### Solutions and colloids
A **solution** (sugar in water) is clear and never settles. A **suspension** (muddy water) is cloudy and settles down.

A **colloid** lies in between. Its particles are too small to see. They still scatter a light beam. This is the **Tyndall effect**. The particles also zig-zag constantly. This is **Brownian motion**.

- Milk is an **emulsion** (liquid in liquid).
- Fog and clouds are an **aerosol** (liquid in gas).
- Smoke is a solid in gas.
- Shaving cream is a foam. Jelly is a gel.

> **Watch:** A true solution does not show the Tyndall effect. Only colloids and suspensions do.

### Inside the atom
| Particle | Found by | Charge |
|---|---|---|
| Electron | J.J. Thomson (1897, cathode rays) | -1 |
| Proton | Goldstein (canal rays); identified by Rutherford | +1 |
| Neutron | James Chadwick (1932) | 0 |

The atomic models came in this order.

1. **Dalton:** atoms cannot be split.
2. **Thomson:** plum-pudding model.
3. **Rutherford:** gold-foil experiment showed a tiny, dense nucleus.
4. **Bohr:** electrons move in fixed orbits (shells).

### Atomic number, isotopes and shells
**Atomic number Z** is the number of protons. **Mass number A** is protons plus neutrons.

- **Isotopes:** same Z, different A. Hydrogen has protium (¹H), deuterium (²H) and tritium (³H). Tritium is radioactive.
- Chlorine is ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. Its average mass is 35.5. Carbon-14 is used to date old remains.
- **Isobars:** same A, different Z. Argon-40 and calcium-40 are an example.
- **Isotones:** same number of neutrons.

Shell n holds at most $2n^{2}$ electrons. So K holds 2, L holds 8 and M holds 18. The outer electrons are the valence electrons.

### The mole and the gas laws
One **mole** holds $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ particles. This is Avogadro's number. One mole weighs its molar mass in grams. So 18 g of water is 1 mole, and 44 g of CO₂ is 1 mole.

- **Boyle's law:** at fixed temperature, $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$.
- **Charles's law:** at fixed pressure, volume rises with kelvin temperature.

> **Rule:** In Charles's law, always change °C to kelvin first. Add 273.

patterns.name: Physical vs chemical change; sublimation and states
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks 'which is a chemical change', 'which sublimes', the 4th or 5th state, or 'dry ice is'.
steps: Ask: is a new substance formed?
Yes: chemical (burning, rusting, curdling, cooking, digestion). No: physical.
For sublimation, pick from camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice.
For states: plasma is ionised gas; BEC is near absolute zero.
patterns.why: The two change types differ only in whether a new substance appears.

example.q: Burning of a candle involves which change?
steps: Melting of wax is physical.
Burning of the vapour is chemical.

patterns.name: Separation method and mixture
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks 'which method separates cream from milk, petroleum parts, or dyes in ink', or gives a match-the-column.
steps: Find the property that differs: boiling point, density, solubility, magnetism.
Close boiling points: fractional distillation. Different densities: centrifugation.
Immiscible liquids: separating funnel. Dyes: chromatography.
Cream from milk is always centrifugation.
patterns.why: Each method uses one physical property that differs between the parts.

example.q: The components of petroleum are separated by which method?
steps: The parts boil only a few degrees apart.
A fractionating column is needed.

patterns.name: Colloids, Tyndall effect and Brownian motion
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'milk is an example of', 'scattering of light by particles is called', or 'which shows the Tyndall effect'.
steps: Name the dispersed phase and the medium.
Liquid in liquid is an emulsion; liquid in gas is an aerosol; solid in gas is smoke.
Light scattering is the Tyndall effect. Zig-zag motion is Brownian motion.
A true solution never shows the Tyndall effect.
patterns.why: Colloid particles are big enough to scatter light but too small to settle.

example.q: Fog is a colloid in which what is spread in what?
steps: Water droplets are liquid.
Air is the gas medium.

patterns.name: Atomic models and discoverers
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks who proposed the plum-pudding, nuclear or orbit model, or which experiment found the nucleus.
steps: Recall the order: Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr, Chadwick.
Thomson: electron and plum pudding. Rutherford: nucleus. Bohr: orbits.
In the gold-foil test most alpha particles passed straight through. A few bounced back.
patterns.why: Each scientist added one part to the picture of the atom.

example.q: Rutherford's gold-foil experiment proved what?
steps: Most alpha particles went straight through.
A few bounced back.
example.answer: The atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus

patterns.name: Isotopes, isobars, atomic number and shells
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'same atomic number, different mass number', asks the hydrogen isotopes, or asks electrons in a shell.
steps: Same Z, different A: isotopes. Same A, different Z: isobars.
Hydrogen isotopes: ¹H, ²H, ³H. Chlorine: ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, average 35.5.
Shell n holds 2n² electrons. Calcium (Z = 20) is 2, 8, 8, 2.
patterns.why: The atomic number sets the element. The mass number only counts the heavier particles.

example.q: How many electrons can the M shell hold at most?
steps: M is the third shell, so n = 3.

patterns.name: Mole and gas-law numericals
patterns.howToSpot: You get a mass and must find moles or molecules, or a Boyle or Charles change of volume, pressure or temperature.
steps: Find the molar mass first: H₂O is 18, CO₂ is 44.
Moles = given mass ÷ molar mass.
Boyle: equate the two products P × V.
Charles: convert to kelvin, then equate V ÷ T.
patterns.why: A mole is a counting unit, and the gas laws are simple proportions.

example.q: A gas takes 600 mL at 1 atm. What pressure squeezes it into 400 mL at the same temperature?
steps: Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.

revision: Five states: solid, liquid, gas, plasma, Bose-Einstein condensate.
Sublimation: camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice.
Chromatography for dyes; fractional distillation for petroleum; centrifuge for cream; funnel for oil and water.
Colloid shows Tyndall effect and Brownian motion. Milk is an emulsion. Fog is an aerosol.
Electron: Thomson. Nucleus: Rutherford. Orbits: Bohr. Neutron: Chadwick.
Shell capacity is 2n². K = 2, L = 8, M = 18.
One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles. 18 g of water = 1 mole. PV = nRT.

subtopics.title: Periodic table, elements and record-holders
subtopics.concept: The periodic table arranges all elements in order of atomic number. Its columns are groups and its rows are periods. Elements in one group behave alike, and properties change in a steady way across a period and down a group. Exams also ask fixed record-holders and Latin-name symbols.

tricks.title: Crust order: OSAIC
tricks.body: Oxygen, Silicon, Aluminium, Iron, Calcium. So the top element is O and the top metal is Al.

example.q: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
steps: Read OSAIC and skip the non-metals O and Si.
The first metal is aluminium.

tricks.title: Two liquids at room temperature
tricks.body: Mercury is the liquid metal. Bromine is the liquid non-metal. Gallium and caesium melt just above room temperature.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Mendeleev's table used atomic number.
mistakes.right: Mendeleev used atomic mass. Moseley used atomic number.

mistakes.wrong: Naming iron as the most abundant metal in the crust.
mistakes.right: It is aluminium. Iron comes second.

mistakes.wrong: Naming oxygen as the most abundant gas in air.
mistakes.right: It is nitrogen, about 78%. Oxygen is about 21%.

mistakes.wrong: Writing the symbol of sodium as So.
mistakes.right: Use the Latin name: natrium gives Na.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking size grows across a period.
mistakes.right: Size falls left to right and rises down a group.

subtopics.notes:
### How the table grew
Chemists needed a map for the elements they kept finding. Four names matter.

| Scientist | Idea |
|---|---|
| Döbereiner | Triads, such as Li, Na, K |
| Newlands | Law of octaves: every 8th element is similar |
| Mendeleev | Table built on atomic mass, with gaps left for unknown elements |
| Moseley | Modern periodic law: properties depend on atomic number |

Mendeleev predicted eka-aluminium and eka-silicon. They turned out to be gallium and germanium.

> **Watch:** Mendeleev used atomic mass. Moseley used atomic number.

### Reading the modern table
The modern table has **18 groups** (vertical) and **7 periods** (horizontal). It names **118 elements**. Elements in one group have the same number of outer electrons, so they behave alike.

| Region | Members |
|---|---|
| Group 1 | Alkali metals: Li, Na, K. Very reactive. |
| Group 2 | Alkaline earth metals: Be, Mg, Ca |
| Groups 3-12 | Transition metals: Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, Au |
| Group 17 | Halogens: F, Cl, Br, I |
| Group 18 | Noble gases: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn |
| Two bottom rows | Lanthanides and actinides |

Noble gases have full outer shells. This is why they are inert.

### Trends in the table
- **Across a period (left to right):** atomic size falls. Metallic character falls. Electronegativity (pull on electrons) rises.
- **Down a group (top to bottom):** atomic size rises. Metallic character rises. Metals get more reactive, so K is wilder than Na.

Sodium is a metal. Chlorine, at the far right, is a non-metal. **Fluorine** is the most electronegative element.

> **Tip:** Picture the table. Reactive non-metals sit at the top right. Reactive metals sit at the bottom left.

### Record-holders
| Record | Answer |
|---|---|
| Most abundant in the universe | Hydrogen |
| Most abundant in Earth's crust | Oxygen, then silicon |
| Most abundant metal in the crust | Aluminium, then iron |
| Most abundant gas in air | Nitrogen (about 78%) |
| Most abundant in the human body | Oxygen (top metal: calcium) |
| Lightest element / lightest metal | Hydrogen / Lithium |
| Liquid metal / liquid non-metal | Mercury / Bromine |
| Metal that melts in the palm | Gallium (about 30 °C) |
| Hardest natural substance | Diamond |
| Softest mineral | Talc |
| Best metal conductor | Silver |
| Most ductile and malleable metal | Gold |
| Highest melting point metal | Tungsten |
| Densest natural element | Osmium |
| First man-made element | Technetium |
| Non-metal that conducts | Graphite |

The crust order is **OSAIC**: Oxygen, Silicon, Aluminium, Iron, Calcium.

### Symbols from Latin names
Some symbols come from Latin names. They are common exam traps.

| Symbol | Latin name | Element |
|---|---|---|
| Na | natrium | Sodium |
| K | kalium | Potassium |
| Fe | ferrum | Iron |
| Cu | cuprum | Copper |
| Ag | argentum | Silver |
| Au | aurum | Gold |
| Pb | plumbum | Lead |
| Sn | stannum | Tin |
| Hg | hydrargyrum | Mercury |
| Sb | stibium | Antimony |
| W | wolfram | Tungsten |

> **Watch:** The symbol for sodium is Na, never So.

### Noble gases and metalloids
- **Helium:** balloons, airships and deep-sea diver breathing mixes.
- **Neon:** advertising signs with an orange-red glow.
- **Argon:** filled inside electric bulbs.
- **Xenon:** flash lamps. **Radon** is radioactive.
- **Metalloids:** boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium.

patterns.name: Element record-holders
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'most abundant', 'lightest metal', 'only liquid metal', 'hardest natural substance' or 'first man-made element'.
steps: Match the phrase to the record table.
Abundance chain: H (universe), O (crust), Al (crust metal), N (air), O (body).
Oddities: Li lightest metal, Hg liquid metal, Br liquid non-metal, graphite conducts.
In odd-one-out questions, check the records first.
patterns.why: These records are fixed facts, so recall is the only route.

example.q: The most abundant metal in the Earth's crust is which?
steps: Oxygen is the top element but not a metal.
Aluminium (about 8%) comes before iron.

patterns.name: Symbols from Latin names
patterns.howToSpot: A list of symbol and element pairs is given, and you must find the wrong pair.
steps: Learn the eleven Latin symbols.
Check each pair against the Latin name.
The wrong pair is almost always one of these eleven.
Other symbols follow the English name (He, Ca, Zn).
patterns.why: The Latin names explain symbols that do not match the English name.

example.q: Which pair is wrong? (a) Fe-Iron (b) Au-Gold (c) Ag-Silver (d) So-Sodium
steps: Sodium comes from natrium.
Its symbol is Na.

patterns.name: History of classification
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks who gave the law of octaves, what Mendeleev's table was based on, or what eka-silicon is now called.
steps: Recall the chain: Döbereiner, Newlands, Mendeleev, Moseley.
Mendeleev used atomic mass and left gaps.
Eka-aluminium became gallium. Eka-silicon became germanium.
Modern periods follow atomic number.
patterns.why: Each step fixed a weakness in the one before it.

example.q: Mendeleev's eka-silicon is today's which element?
steps: Mendeleev left a gap under silicon.
The element found later fits that gap.

patterns.name: Groups, periods and trends
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks how size or metallic character changes across a period or down a group, or how many groups exist.
steps: Remember the fixed numbers: 18 groups, 7 periods, 118 elements.
Across a period: size and metallic character fall.
Down a group: size and metallic character rise.
Most reactive non-metal is F. Most reactive metals are at the bottom left.
patterns.why: More shells down a group put the outer electrons farther away, so they leave easily.

example.q: Moving down a group, what happens to metallic character?
steps: Outer electrons are farther from the nucleus.
They are lost more easily, so K is more reactive than Na.

patterns.name: Group families (alkali, halogens, noble gases)
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which group holds halogens or noble gases, why group 18 is inert, or which metal is kept in kerosene.
steps: Group 1 is alkali: Li, Na, K. They are soft, reactive and kept in kerosene.
Group 17 is halogens: F, Cl, Br, I.
Group 18 is noble gases with full outer shells.
Helium is first in group 18. Radon is radioactive.
patterns.why: A full outer shell means the atom has no need to give, take or share electrons.

example.q: Why are noble gases chemically inert?
steps: Look at the outer shell.
It is already complete.
example.answer: Their outer shells are full, so they do not give, take or share electrons easily

revision: Döbereiner triads, Newlands octaves, Mendeleev atomic mass, Moseley atomic number.
18 groups, 7 periods, 118 elements.
Group 1 alkali, group 2 alkaline earth, group 17 halogens, group 18 noble gases.
Across a period size and metallic character fall. Down a group both rise.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
Hydrogen: universe. Oxygen: crust. Aluminium: crust metal. Nitrogen: air.
Li lightest metal, Hg liquid metal, Br liquid non-metal, Au most ductile, W highest melting point.

subtopics.title: Acids, bases, pH, common compounds and reactions
subtopics.concept: Acids taste sour and bases feel slippery. Indicators and the pH scale tell them apart. This lesson also holds the fixed tables that exams love: natural acids, common names of chemicals, and a few everyday reactions.

tricks.title: Kitchen acid map
tricks.body: Vinegar-Acetic, Lemon-Citric, Tamarind-Tartaric, Tomato-Oxalic, Curd-Lactic, Apple-Malic, Ant-Formic. Matching first letters helps: Tamarind and Tartaric, Formica (Latin for ant) and Formic.

example.q: Which acid is present in tomato?
steps: Tomato and spinach share one acid.
That acid is oxalic.

tricks.title: Vitriol colours by metal
tricks.body: Blue vitriol is copper sulphate. Green is iron (ferrous) sulphate. White is zinc sulphate. Oil of vitriol is H₂SO₄.

mistakes.wrong: Swapping baking soda and washing soda.
mistakes.right: Baking soda is NaHCO₃. Washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

mistakes.wrong: Writing aqua regia as 3 HNO₃ : 1 HCl.
mistakes.right: It is 1 part HNO₃ to 3 parts HCl.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking rust forms in dry air.
mistakes.right: Rust needs both oxygen and moisture.

mistakes.wrong: Saying tamarind has citric acid.
mistakes.right: Tamarind has tartaric acid. Citric acid is in lemon.

mistakes.wrong: Removing permanent hardness by boiling.
mistakes.right: Boiling removes only temporary hardness. Use washing soda for permanent hardness.

subtopics.notes:
### Acids, bases and indicators
An **acid** releases H⁺ ions in water and tastes sour. A **base** releases OH⁻ ions and feels slippery. A base that dissolves in water is an **alkali**.

| Indicator | In acid | In base |
|---|---|---|
| Litmus | Blue turns red | Red turns blue |
| Phenolphthalein | Colourless | Pink |
| Methyl orange | Red | Yellow |
| Turmeric | Yellow (no change) | Reddish-brown |

> **Tip:** Phenolphthalein is pink only in a base. In acid it stays colourless.

### The pH scale
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is basic. Each step is a ten-fold change in H⁺.

| Item | pH |
|---|---|
| Gastric juice (HCl) | about 1.2 to 2 |
| Lemon juice | about 2 to 2.5 |
| Pure water | 7 |
| Human blood | about 7.4 (slightly basic) |
| Milk of magnesia | about 10 |

- Tooth decay starts when mouth pH falls below about 5.5.
- Acid rain has pH below about 5.6.
- Antacids such as milk of magnesia neutralise extra stomach acid.
- An ant or bee sting injects formic acid. Rub baking soda on it. A wasp sting is alkaline, so use vinegar.

### Natural sources of acids
| Source | Acid |
|---|---|
| Vinegar | Acetic |
| Lemon, orange | Citric |
| Tamarind, grapes | Tartaric |
| Tomato, spinach | Oxalic |
| Curd, sour milk | Lactic |
| Apple | Malic |
| Ant sting, nettle | Formic |
| Stomach | Hydrochloric |

### Common names and formulae
| Common name | Chemical name and formula |
|---|---|
| Baking soda | Sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃ |
| Washing soda | Na₂CO₃·10H₂O |
| Bleaching powder | Calcium oxychloride, CaOCl₂ |
| Plaster of Paris | CaSO₄·½H₂O |
| Gypsum | CaSO₄·2H₂O |
| Quicklime / slaked lime | CaO / Ca(OH)₂ |
| Limestone, marble, chalk | CaCO₃ |
| Caustic soda / caustic potash | NaOH / KOH |
| Blue vitriol | CuSO₄·5H₂O |
| Green vitriol | FeSO₄·7H₂O |
| White vitriol | ZnSO₄·7H₂O |
| Oil of vitriol | H₂SO₄ |
| Muriatic acid | HCl |
| Epsom salt | MgSO₄·7H₂O |
| Potash alum (fitkari) | K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O, purifies water |
| Hypo | Na₂S₂O₃, used in photography |
| Laughing gas | N₂O |
| Marsh gas | CH₄ |
| Lunar caustic | AgNO₃ |
| Heavy water | D₂O |
| Dry ice | Solid CO₂ |
| Aqua regia | Conc. HNO₃ : conc. HCl in 1 : 3; dissolves gold and platinum |

> **Watch:** Aqua regia is 1 part HNO₃ to 3 parts HCl. Do not reverse it.

### Reactions in daily life
- **Neutralisation:** acid + base gives salt + water.
- **Acid + carbonate** gives salt, water and CO₂. CO₂ turns lime water milky. This is the standard CO₂ test.
- **Oxidation** is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons. **Reduction** is the opposite.
- **Rusting** needs both oxygen and moisture. Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.
- **Rancidity** is oxidation of fats and oils. Chips packets are flushed with nitrogen to stop it.
- **Hard water:** boiling removes temporary hardness (bicarbonates). Washing soda or ion exchange removes permanent hardness (chlorides and sulphates).
- **Chlor-alkali process:** electrolysis of brine gives NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.
- **Plaster of Paris** sets into gypsum when water is added. It is used for casts on broken bones.
- **Water of crystallisation:** CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue. Heating drives off the water and it turns white. Adding water brings the blue back.

patterns.name: Common name and chemical formula
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'baking soda is', 'chemical name of washing soda', 'which is CaO', or gives a formula for a common name.
steps: Learn the table in pairs.
Baking soda NaHCO₃ pairs with washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
Quicklime CaO, lime water Ca(OH)₂, limestone CaCO₃.
Gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O loses water to give plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O.
patterns.why: These names are fixed by tradition, so recall by pairs is the only route.

example.q: What is the chemical formula of baking soda?
steps: Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate.
Washing soda is the other one, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

patterns.name: Natural source and acid
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'tamarind contains', 'the acid in an ant sting', or gives a match-the-column of foods and acids.
steps: Recall the kitchen map.
Tamarind and grapes: tartaric. Tomato and spinach: oxalic. Apple: malic.
Ant sting and nettle: formic. Curd: lactic. Stomach: hydrochloric.
For a sting, use baking soda to neutralise.
patterns.why: Each food has one main acid that gives its sour taste.

example.q: Which acid is present in tamarind?
steps: Tamarind is not citrus.
Grapes share its acid.

patterns.name: Indicators and pH values
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks 'phenolphthalein turns pink in', turmeric with a base, the pH of blood, or whether a given pH is acidic.
steps: Recall the indicator colours.
pH below 7 is acid, 7 is neutral, above 7 is base.
Blood is about 7.4. Tooth enamel dissolves below pH 5.5.
A lower pH means a stronger acid. Each unit is ten times.
patterns.why: The pH scale counts hydrogen ions on a log scale, so one step means ten times.

example.q: Solution A has pH 3 and solution B has pH 5. How much more acidic is A?
steps: The pH differs by 2 units.
Each unit is ten times, so 10 × 10 = 100.

patterns.name: Salt chemistry and standard reactions
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'CO₂ turns lime water', 'plaster of Paris is made from', chlor-alkali products, or quicklime with water.
steps: Acid plus carbonate gives CO₂.
CO₂ with lime water gives white CaCO₃, which looks milky.
Heated gypsum gives plaster of Paris. Water sets it back to gypsum.
Brine electrolysis gives NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.
patterns.why: Each of these is a fixed reaction, so link the input to the product.

example.q: Why does lime water turn milky when CO₂ is passed through it?
steps: CO₂ reacts with Ca(OH)₂.
Insoluble CaCO₃ forms.
example.answer: Calcium carbonate forms, a standard test for CO₂

patterns.name: Uses of baking soda, washing soda, bleaching powder
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which chemical is an antacid, removes hardness, or disinfects water, or why cakes rise.
steps: Baking soda: antacid, baking powder, soda-acid extinguisher.
Washing soda: removes permanent hardness; used for glass and borax.
Bleaching powder: disinfects drinking water, bleaches cotton.
Match the job to the chemical.
patterns.why: Each chemical has a few well-known uses. Exams test only those.

example.q: Permanent hardness of water is removed by adding which chemical?
steps: Permanent hardness comes from chlorides and sulphates.
Washing soda precipitates calcium and magnesium.

patterns.name: Vitriols and water of crystallisation
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks 'oil of vitriol is', 'blue vitriol is', or why blue copper sulphate turns white on heating.
steps: Recall: oil is H₂SO₄, blue is CuSO₄·5H₂O, green is FeSO₄·7H₂O, white is ZnSO₄·7H₂O.
The dot-water is water of crystallisation.
Heating drives it off. Moistening restores it.
patterns.why: Fixed water molecules inside the crystal cause its colour.

example.q: Blue vitriol (CuSO₄·5H₂O) is heated strongly. What colour does it turn?
steps: It loses its five waters.
The anhydrous salt is white.
example.answer: White; adding water turns it blue again

revision: pH below 7 acid, 7 neutral, above 7 base. Blood is 7.4.
Tooth decay starts below pH 5.5. Acid rain is below about 5.6.
Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in base.
Ant sting: formic acid. Tamarind: tartaric. Tomato: oxalic.
Baking soda NaHCO₃. Washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O. Caustic soda NaOH.
Gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O gives plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O.
Milky lime water means CO₂. Aqua regia is HNO₃ : HCl = 1 : 3.

subtopics.title: Metals, ores, metallurgy and alloys
subtopics.concept: Metals shine, bend and carry electricity, and a few exceptions are popular exam picks. This lesson pairs each metal with its ore, walks through the steps of extraction, and lists the reactivity series and alloy recipes. It ends with rusting and gold purity.

tricks.title: Reactivity series sentence
tricks.body: Please Stop Calling Me A Zebra, I Like Her Calling Me Smart Goat gives Potassium, Sodium, Calcium, Magnesium, Aluminium, Zinc, Iron, Lead, Hydrogen, Copper, Mercury, Silver, Gold.

tricks.title: Brass or bronze
tricks.body: Brass has zinc. Bronze has tin. Both have copper.

example.q: Bronze is an alloy of which metals?
steps: Bronze is a copper alloy.
The partner metal is tin.

mistakes.wrong: Believing German silver contains silver.
mistakes.right: It is copper, zinc and nickel.

mistakes.wrong: Naming haematite as an aluminium ore.
mistakes.right: Haematite is iron. Bauxite is aluminium.

mistakes.wrong: Saying solder has a high melting point.
mistakes.right: Solder melts easily. That is why it joins wires.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up calcination and roasting.
mistakes.right: Calcination is for carbonates in limited air. Roasting is for sulphides in excess air.

mistakes.wrong: Saying brass is copper and tin.
mistakes.right: Brass is copper and zinc. Bronze is copper and tin.

subtopics.notes:
### Metals and non-metals
Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile and sonorous. They conduct heat and electricity. Non-metals are mostly dull, brittle and poor conductors.

The exceptions are the exam favourites.

- **Mercury** is a liquid metal.
- **Sodium and potassium** are soft metals. A knife cuts them.
- **Graphite** is a non-metal that conducts electricity.
- **Iodine** is a lustrous non-metal.
- **Diamond** is the hardest natural substance, and it is a non-metal.

### Ore and metal
| Metal | Main ore |
|---|---|
| Aluminium | Bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O) |
| Iron | Haematite (Fe₂O₃), magnetite (Fe₃O₄), siderite |
| Copper | Copper pyrites (chalcopyrite), malachite, cuprite |
| Zinc | Zinc blende (ZnS), calamine |
| Lead | Galena (PbS) |
| Mercury | Cinnabar (HgS) |
| Tin | Cassiterite (SnO₂) |
| Uranium | Pitchblende |
| Silver | Argentite |
| Sodium | Rock salt |
| Magnesium | Magnesite, dolomite, carnallite |
| Calcium | Limestone, gypsum |

### Extracting a metal
Metallurgy has four steps.

1. **Concentration.** Froth flotation suits sulphide ores. Pine oil is used. Magnetic and gravity separation also work.
2. **Convert to oxide.** Calcination heats a carbonate ore in limited air. Roasting heats a sulphide ore in excess air.
3. **Reduction.** Carbon reduces iron in the blast furnace. Very reactive metals need electrolysis: aluminium (Hall-Héroult process), sodium, potassium.
4. **Refining.** In electrolytic refining the impure metal is the anode. Pure metal collects on the cathode. Copper is refined this way.

> **Tip:** Calcination goes with carbonate. Roasting goes with sulphide.

### The reactivity series
$$\text{K} > \text{Na} > \text{Ca} > \text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Zn} > \text{Fe} > \text{Pb} > (\text{H}) > \text{Cu} > \text{Hg} > \text{Ag} > \text{Au}$$

- Metals above hydrogen give H₂ with dilute acids. Copper, silver and gold do not.
- Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene. White phosphorus is stored under water.
- Gold and platinum are noble metals. They occur free in nature.
- A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution. An iron nail in copper sulphate turns brown.

### Rusting and corrosion
Rusting needs **both air and moisture**. Rust is hydrated iron oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

- **Prevention:** galvanisation (zinc coating), painting, greasing, electroplating, and alloying into stainless steel.
- Silver tarnishes black (Ag₂S). Copper grows a green coat of basic copper carbonate.
- Aluminium protects itself with a thin oxide film. Anodising makes it thicker.

### Alloys
| Alloy | Made of | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Brass | Copper + zinc | Utensils, fittings |
| Bronze | Copper + tin | Statues, medals |
| Bell metal | Copper + more tin | Bells, gongs |
| Gun metal | Copper + tin + zinc | Gears, castings |
| German silver | Copper + zinc + nickel (no silver) | Utensils |
| Solder | Lead + tin | Joins wires; low melting point |
| Stainless steel | Iron + chromium + nickel + carbon | Cutlery |
| Duralumin | Aluminium + copper + magnesium + manganese | Aircraft |
| Magnalium | Aluminium + magnesium | Light instruments |
| Nichrome | Nickel + chromium | Heater coils |
| Invar | Iron + nickel | Pendulums, tapes |
| Amalgam | Any metal + mercury | Dental fillings |

### Gold purity
24 carat is pure gold. Use $\text{Purity}\,(\%) = \dfrac{\text{carat}}{24} \times 100$. So 18 carat is 75%, and 22 carat is about 91.67%. Jewellery gold is mixed with copper or silver to make it hard.

patterns.name: Ore and metal matching
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'bauxite is the ore of', 'cinnabar is an ore of', or gives a match-the-column of ores and metals.
steps: Learn the headline pairs: bauxite-Al, haematite-Fe, cinnabar-Hg, galena-Pb.
Add zinc blende-Zn, cassiterite-Sn, copper pyrites-Cu, pitchblende-U, rock salt-Na.
Extra ores: calamine is zinc; magnetite and siderite are iron.
In a match, fix the surest pair first and chain the rest.
patterns.why: Ore names are fixed, so recall by pairs works better than logic.

example.q: Cinnabar is an ore of which metal?
steps: Cinnabar is HgS.
Hg is mercury.

patterns.name: Alloy and composition
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks 'brass is an alloy of', 'which alloy contains tin', or what is added to iron for stainless steel.
steps: Copper family: brass Cu + Zn, bronze Cu + Sn, bell metal Cu + more Sn, German silver Cu + Zn + Ni.
Iron family: stainless steel Fe + Cr + Ni, invar Fe + Ni.
Others: duralumin Al + Cu, magnalium Al + Mg, solder Pb + Sn, nichrome Ni + Cr.
Amalgam always has mercury.
patterns.why: Each alloy has a fixed recipe, and the second metal is what exams test.

example.q: Brass is an alloy of which metals?
steps: Brass is a copper alloy.
The partner is zinc, not tin.

patterns.name: Metallurgy steps and processes
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'roasting is used for', 'calcination vs roasting', 'froth flotation', or 'which metal is extracted by electrolysis'.
steps: Concentrate the ore. Froth flotation is for sulphide ores.
Calcination: carbonate ore, limited air. Roasting: sulphide ore, excess air.
Reduce with carbon (iron) or by electrolysis (Al, Na).
Refine copper electrolytically with the impure metal as the anode.
patterns.why: Each step prepares the ore for the next, from ore to pure metal.

example.q: Roasting is done for which type of ore?
steps: Roasting uses excess air.
It turns sulphides into oxides and drives off SO₂.

patterns.name: Reactivity series consequences
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which metal gives no H₂ with dilute acid, why sodium is kept in kerosene, or which metal occurs free.
steps: Write the series: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au.
Metals above H give H₂ with dilute acids.
Top metals burn in moist air, so keep them under kerosene.
Bottom metals occur free. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one.
patterns.why: Position in the series tells you how eagerly a metal reacts.

example.q: Which metal will not liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
steps: Find hydrogen in the series.
Copper lies below it.

patterns.name: Corrosion and its prevention
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'rusting requires', 'galvanisation is coating with', 'green coating on copper', or 'anodising is done on'.
steps: Rusting needs air and moisture together.
Prevent with galvanising, paint, oil, electroplating, anodising or alloying.
Colours: iron is red-brown rust; copper is green; silver is black.
patterns.why: Each prevention method keeps air or water away from the metal.

example.q: A green coating slowly forms on a copper vessel left in damp air. What is it?
steps: Copper reacts slowly with moist air.
It forms basic copper carbonate.
example.answer: Basic copper carbonate (silver turns black with Ag₂S)

patterns.name: Metal and non-metal exceptions, gold carat
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which metal is liquid or soft, which non-metal conducts, the most ductile metal, or a carat purity.
steps: Exceptions: Hg liquid; Na and K soft; graphite conducts; iodine lustrous.
Best metal conductor: silver. Most ductile: gold. Highest melting point: tungsten.
Purity = carat ÷ 24 × 100.
patterns.why: The exceptions break the general rule, so questions love them.

example.q: Which non-metal conducts electricity?
steps: Carbon layers in graphite hold free electrons.
These carry current.

revision: Calcination: carbonate. Roasting: sulphide. Froth flotation: sulphide ores.
Bauxite: Al. Haematite: Fe. Cinnabar: Hg. Zinc blende: Zn. Galena: Pb. Cassiterite: Sn. Pitchblende: U.
K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
Cu, Ag and Au give no H₂ with dilute acid.
Brass: Cu + Zn. Bronze: Cu + Sn. Solder: Pb + Sn. Duralumin: Al + Cu. Nichrome: Ni + Cr.
Rusting needs air and moisture. Galvanising is a zinc coat.
Amalgam is a metal with mercury. 24 carat is pure gold.

subtopics.title: Carbon compounds, fuels, polymers, industry and pollution
subtopics.concept: Carbon forms long chains, so it makes millions of compounds. This lesson covers carbon forms, fuels, polymers, factory processes and pollution. Nearly every question asks you to match a name to its product, use or effect.

tricks.title: Process to product
tricks.body: Haber gives ammonia. Contact gives sulphuric acid. Ostwald gives nitric acid. Solvay gives soda. Catalysts: Haber Fe, Contact V₂O₅, Ostwald Pt.

example.q: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process?
steps: The Contact process makes sulphuric acid.
Its catalyst is vanadium pentoxide.

tricks.title: Japanese diseases
tricks.body: Minamata goes with mercury. Itai-itai (bone pain) goes with cadmium.

mistakes.wrong: Saying LPG is mainly methane.
mistakes.right: LPG is mainly butane. CNG and biogas are mainly methane.

mistakes.wrong: Calling Bakelite a thermoplastic.
mistakes.right: Bakelite is thermosetting.

mistakes.wrong: Naming phosgene for the Bhopal tragedy.
mistakes.right: The gas was methyl isocyanate (MIC).

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up methanol and ethanol.
mistakes.right: Methanol is poisonous. Ethanol is the drinking alcohol.

mistakes.wrong: Saying detergent forms scum in hard water.
mistakes.right: Soap forms scum. Detergents work in hard water.

subtopics.notes:
### Carbon and its forms
Carbon joins to itself in chains and rings. This is **catenation**. Its valency is 4, called tetravalency.

**Allotropes** are different forms of one element.

- **Diamond:** hardest natural substance. It does not conduct.
- **Graphite:** soft and slippery. It conducts electricity. It is used in pencils, electrodes and lubricants.
- **Fullerene (C₆₀):** a ball of 60 carbon atoms.
- **Graphene:** a single layer of graphite.

### Hydrocarbons
| Family | Bonds | General formula |
|---|---|---|
| Alkane | Single, saturated | $C_nH_{2n+2}$ |
| Alkene | One double bond | $C_nH_{2n}$ |
| Alkyne | One triple bond | $C_nH_{2n-2}$ |

Methane (CH₄) is the simplest alkane. Ethene is an alkene. Ethyne (acetylene, C₂H₂) is an alkyne.

### Fuels
| Fuel | Main component |
|---|---|
| CNG | Methane |
| LPG | Butane (with propane) |
| Biogas (gobar gas) | Methane, plus CO₂ |
| Oxy-acetylene flame | Ethyne (acetylene), for welding and cutting |
| Water gas | CO + H₂ |
| Producer gas | CO + N₂ |

- LPG has no smell. **Ethyl mercaptan** is added so a leak can be smelt.
- Hydrogen has the highest calorific value by mass.
- Octane number rates petrol. Cetane number rates diesel.
- Coal ranks by carbon: peat, lignite, bituminous, anthracite. Anthracite is best.
- Fractional distillation splits petroleum into refinery gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil and bitumen.
- Ethylene ripens fruit. Calcium carbide is banned for this.

### Everyday carbon compounds
- **Methanol** is poisonous. It can cause blindness. **Ethanol** is the alcohol in drinks and is blended with petrol.
- **Vinegar** is about 5 to 8% acetic acid.
- **Esters** give fruits their smell.
- **Soap** is a sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid. **Saponification** (fat + NaOH) makes it.
- Soap forms scum in hard water. **Detergents** work in hard water too.
- **Hydrogenation** of vegetable oil uses a nickel catalyst. It gives vanaspati ghee.

> **Watch:** Methanol is poison. Ethanol is the drinking alcohol.

### Polymers
A polymer is a giant molecule made of repeating units.

| Polymer | Note |
|---|---|
| Polythene | From ethene; bags |
| PVC | From vinyl chloride; pipes |
| Teflon | From tetrafluoroethylene; non-stick cookware |
| Bakelite | Phenol + formaldehyde; first plastic; thermosetting; switches |
| Nylon | First fully synthetic fibre |
| Natural rubber | Polyisoprene |
| Rayon | Artificial silk from cellulose |
| Melamine | Thermosetting; crockery |

- **Vulcanisation** heats rubber with sulphur (Charles Goodyear). It makes rubber hard and elastic.
- **Thermoplastics** (polythene, PVC) soften on heating. **Thermosetting plastics** (Bakelite, melamine) do not.

### Factory processes
| Process | Product | Catalyst |
|---|---|---|
| Haber | Ammonia | Iron |
| Contact | Sulphuric acid | Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) |
| Ostwald | Nitric acid | Platinum |
| Solvay | Sodium carbonate | none |
| Chlor-alkali | NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂ from brine | none |

Glass is silica (sand), sodium carbonate and limestone fused together. Borosilicate (Pyrex) resists heat. Portland cement was made by Joseph Aspdin. Gypsum is added to slow its setting.

### Pollution and poisons
| Substance | Effect |
|---|---|
| SO₂, NO₂ | Acid rain; damage to the Taj Mahal |
| CFCs | Ozone layer depletion |
| CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour | Greenhouse effect |
| Carbon monoxide | Binds haemoglobin; suffocation |
| Methyl isocyanate (MIC) | Bhopal gas tragedy, 1984 |
| Mercury | Minamata disease, Japan |
| Cadmium | Itai-itai disease, Japan |
| Arsenic | Black-foot disease; groundwater |
| Excess fluoride | Fluorosis of teeth and bones |
| Nitrate in water | Blue baby syndrome |
| Lead | Plumbism |

> **Tip:** Minamata starts with M, like Mercury. Itai-itai means ouch-ouch, and cadmium is the cause.

patterns.name: Fuel and main component
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'CNG is mainly', 'LPG contains', 'why does LPG smell', 'gas used in welding' or 'best coal'.
steps: CNG and biogas are methane.
LPG is butane with propane. Ethyl mercaptan gives it a smell.
Welding uses acetylene (ethyne) with oxygen.
Coal ranking: peat, lignite, bituminous, anthracite.
patterns.why: Each fuel is a named hydrocarbon, so the answer is recall plus one use.

example.q: Which gas is used with oxygen in a welding torch?
steps: The flame must be very hot.
The gas is ethyne.

patterns.name: Industrial process and product
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Haber process gives', 'sulphuric acid is made by', or gives a match-the-column of processes and chemicals.
steps: Fix four pairs: Haber-ammonia, Contact-sulphuric acid, Ostwald-nitric acid, Solvay-sodium carbonate.
Add catalysts: Haber iron, Contact V₂O₅, Ostwald platinum.
Anchor on ammonia and eliminate the rest.
patterns.why: Each process is named after its inventor or its method and is fixed.

example.q: The Contact process makes which chemical?
steps: SO₂ is oxidised to SO₃ over V₂O₅.
SO₃ is absorbed to make the acid.

patterns.name: Polymers, plastics and fibres
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks the first synthetic fibre, the first plastic, a use of Teflon, or what vulcanisation uses.
steps: Records: nylon is the first fully synthetic fibre. Bakelite is the first plastic.
Uses: polythene bags, PVC pipes, Teflon non-stick, nylon ropes and parachutes.
Vulcanisation is natural rubber with sulphur.
Cotton is cellulose. Silk and wool are protein.
patterns.why: Polymers are named for their monomer or their use, and exams test both.

example.q: Vulcanised rubber is made by heating natural rubber with what?
steps: Goodyear found the method.
The added element is sulphur.

patterns.name: Allotropes and hydrocarbon families
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which carbon form conducts, the hardest natural substance, a general formula, or which hydrocarbon is saturated.
steps: Diamond is hardest and does not conduct. Graphite conducts.
Alkane $C_nH_{2n+2}$ is saturated. Alkene $C_nH_{2n}$. Alkyne $C_nH_{2n-2}$.
Methane is the simplest alkane.
patterns.why: A double or triple bond takes the place of hydrogen atoms, so the formula loses hydrogens.

example.q: Which general formula belongs to an alkyne?
steps: An alkyne has a triple bond.
Acetylene C₂H₂ fits $C_nH_{2n-2}$ with n = 2.

patterns.name: Everyday carbon chemistry
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which alcohol causes blindness, what vinegar contains, why soap fails in hard water, or the catalyst for hydrogenation.
steps: Methanol is poison. Ethanol is drinkable.
Vinegar is 5 to 8% acetic acid.
Soap is made by saponification and forms scum in hard water.
Hydrogenation of oil uses nickel and gives vanaspati.
patterns.why: Each item links one chemical to one everyday fact.

example.q: Why does soap not lather well in hard water?
steps: Hard water has calcium and magnesium ions.
They react with soap to form insoluble scum.
example.answer: Scum forms; detergents work even in hard water

patterns.name: Pollutant and disease or event
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Minamata disease is caused by', 'which gas causes acid rain', 'CFCs damage', or 'Bhopal gas leaked'.
steps: Minamata: mercury. Itai-itai: cadmium.
CO binds haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen.
SO₂ and NOₓ cause acid rain. CFCs harm the ozone layer (Montreal Protocol 1987).
Bhopal 1984 was methyl isocyanate. Greenhouse gases: CO₂, CH₄.
patterns.why: Each pollutant harms one target, and exams pair them.

example.q: Minamata disease resulted from poisoning by which metal?
steps: Factory waste in Japan entered fish.
The pollutant was mercury.

revision: CNG and biogas: methane. LPG: butane with ethyl mercaptan for smell. Welding: acetylene.
Anthracite is the best coal.
Haber: NH₃. Contact: H₂SO₄. Ostwald: HNO₃. Solvay: Na₂CO₃.
Nylon is the first synthetic fibre. Bakelite is the first plastic.
Vulcanisation is rubber plus sulphur. Teflon is non-stick.
Hydrogenation uses a nickel catalyst. Soap scums in hard water.
CO binds haemoglobin. Minamata: Hg. Itai-itai: Cd. CFC: ozone. Bhopal: MIC, 1984.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Baking soda is chemically..." or "formula of plaster of Paris".
pyqPatterns.approach:
Baking soda = NaHCO₃, washing soda = Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, caustic soda = NaOH.
Quicklime = CaO, limestone = CaCO₃, gypsum = CaSO₄·2H₂O.

example.q: What is plaster of Paris chemically?
example.solution:
Gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O
Heating gypsum removes most of its water
What is left is CaSO₄·½H₂O, plaster of Paris
**CaSO₄·½H₂O**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "The acid in tamarind / curd / lemon / ant sting is..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Vinegar = acetic, lemon = citric, tamarind = tartaric, tomato = oxalic.
Curd = lactic, ant sting = formic.

example.q: Which acid is present in an ant sting?
example.solution:
Ants inject a stinging liquid
The liquid contains formic acid
A mild base like baking soda soothes it
**Formic acid**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Phenolphthalein is colourless in..." or "which solution is more acidic".
pyqPatterns.approach:
Litmus turns red in acid. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base.
pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is basic.

example.q: What colour does phenolphthalein show in a base?
example.solution:
In acid it is colourless
In base it changes colour
Remember: Pink in Base
**Pink**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Ore to metal, alloy to metals
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Bauxite is the ore of..." or "brass is an alloy of..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Ores: bauxite = aluminium, haematite = iron, galena = lead, cinnabar = mercury.
Alloys: brass = Cu + Zn, bronze = Cu + Sn, solder = Pb + Sn.

example.q: Brass is an alloy of which metals?
example.solution:
Both brass and bronze contain copper
Brass has zinc with it
Bronze has tin with it (the usual wrong option)
**Copper and zinc**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Father of the periodic table" or "symbol of sodium / gold / iron".
pyqPatterns.approach:
Mendeleev made the periodic table; Moseley fixed the modern one by atomic number.
Latin symbols: Na (natrium), K (kalium), Au (aurum), Fe (ferrum).

example.q: What is the chemical symbol of sodium?
example.solution:
The Latin name of sodium is natrium
Take the first two letters
That gives Na
**Na**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "The Haber process gives..." or "CNG mainly contains..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Haber = ammonia, Contact = sulphuric acid, Ostwald = nitric acid, Solvay = sodium carbonate.
CNG and biogas = methane.

example.q: The Solvay process is used to make which compound?
example.solution:
Haber gives ammonia
Contact gives sulphuric acid
Solvay gives washing soda (sodium carbonate)
**Sodium carbonate**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Pollutant and the harm it causes
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Minamata disease is caused by..." or "acid rain is caused by..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Minamata = mercury, itai-itai = cadmium (both Japan).
Bhopal 1984 = methyl isocyanate, acid rain = SO₂ and NOₓ, ozone hole = CFCs.

example.q: Minamata disease is caused by poisoning with which metal?
example.solution:
Minamata is a bay in Japan
Fish there were poisoned by factory waste
The poison was mercury
**Mercury**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Who discovered the electron / neutron?" or "isotopes differ in..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Electron = J.J. Thomson, proton = Goldstein, neutron = Chadwick, nucleus = Rutherford.
Atomic number = number of protons. Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons.

example.q: Isotopes of an element differ in the number of what?
example.solution:
Isotopes are atoms of the same element
So their protons are equal
Their mass numbers differ, so their neutrons differ
**Neutrons**

solvedExamples.q: What is the chemical formula of Plaster of Paris?
solvedExamples.solution: **Plaster of Paris** is calcium sulphate **hemihydrate**, CaSO₄·½H₂O, made by heating gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) to about 373 K. On mixing with water it sets back into gypsum. CaCO₃ is limestone and CaOCl₂ is bleaching powder.

solvedExamples.q: What is the percentage of pure gold in 22-carat gold (approximately)?
solvedExamples.solution: 24 carat is pure gold, so 22 carat = 22/24 × 100 = **91.67%**. The rest is usually copper or silver for hardness.

solvedExamples.q: Which gas leaked in the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984?
solvedExamples.solution: On the night of 2–3 December 1984, **methyl isocyanate (MIC)** leaked from the Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, causing one of the world's worst industrial disasters.
**Brass = copper + zinc.** Copper + tin is **bronze**, and lead + tin is **solder**.

practice.q: The chemical name of baking soda is:
practice.solution: Baking soda is **sodium hydrogen carbonate (sodium bicarbonate), NaHCO₃**. Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) is washing soda, and sodium hydroxide is caustic soda.

practice.q: Which acid is present in tamarind?
practice.solution: Tamarind contains **tartaric acid**. Citrus fruits have citric acid, tomato has oxalic acid and curd has lactic acid.

practice.q: The pH of human blood is approximately:
practice.solution: Human blood is **slightly basic, about pH 7.4** (normal range about 7.35–7.45), kept steady by buffer systems.

practice.q: What colour does phenolphthalein show in a basic solution?
practice.solution: Phenolphthalein is **colourless in acidic and neutral** solutions and turns **pink in basic** solutions.

practice.q: Bauxite is the chief ore of:
practice.solution: **Bauxite** (hydrated aluminium oxide) is the chief ore of **aluminium**, extracted by electrolysis (Hall–Héroult process).

practice.q: Solder, used for joining electrical wires, is an alloy of:
practice.solution: **Solder = lead + tin.** Its low melting point lets it melt easily and join wires. Copper + zinc is brass, copper + tin is bronze.

practice.q: Which metal is stored under kerosene to prevent it from reacting with air and moisture?
practice.solution: **Sodium** (and potassium) react vigorously with oxygen and water — sodium can catch fire — so they are kept **under kerosene**. White phosphorus, a non-metal, is stored under water.

practice.q: Which metal is a liquid at normal room temperature?
practice.solution: **Mercury** is the metal that is liquid at room temperature. **Bromine** is also liquid but is a **non-metal**. Gallium melts at about 30 °C — in the palm — but is solid at a normal room temperature of about 25 °C.
practice.shortcut: Liquid metal = Hg; liquid non-metal = Br.

practice.q: The modern periodic table is based on:
practice.solution: Henry **Moseley** showed that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their **atomic number**, which is the basis of the modern periodic law. Mendeleev's table was based on atomic mass.

practice.q: Isotopes of an element have the same:
practice.solution: **Isotopes** have the **same atomic number** (protons) but **different mass numbers** because their neutron counts differ. Their chemical properties are similar; physical properties such as density differ.

practice.q: Which of the following substances undergoes sublimation?
practice.solution: **Camphor** changes directly from solid to vapour — **sublimation**. Naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride and dry ice also sublime.

practice.q: The Haber process is used for the manufacture of:
practice.solution: The **Haber process** combines nitrogen and hydrogen over an **iron catalyst** to make **ammonia**. Sulphuric acid comes from the Contact process, nitric acid from the Ostwald process and sodium carbonate from the Solvay process.

practice.q: Teflon, used in non-stick cookware, is a polymer of:
practice.solution: **Teflon** is polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), made from **tetrafluoroethylene**. Vinyl chloride gives PVC, isoprene gives natural rubber and ethene gives polythene.

practice.q: The main constituent of CNG (compressed natural gas) is:
practice.solution: CNG is mostly **methane**. LPG is mainly **butane** with propane.

practice.q: Minamata disease is caused by poisoning from:
practice.solution: **Minamata disease** (Japan, 1950s) was caused by **methylmercury** in industrial wastewater, which accumulated in fish. Cadmium caused itai-itai disease.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **chemical** change?
practice.solution: Rusting forms a **new substance (iron oxide)** and cannot be reversed by simple means. Melting, dissolving and boiling change only the form — physical changes.

practice.q: **Dry ice** is —
practice.solution: **Dry ice** is solid CO₂, which sublimes directly into gas — used for cooling and stage effects.

practice.q: Which of the following does **NOT** sublime?
practice.solution: The sublimation set is **camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride and dry ice**. Common salt stays solid and is separated from camphor exactly by sublimation.

practice.q: **Cream is separated from milk** by —
practice.solution: Spinning in a **centrifuge** throws the denser skimmed milk outward and collects the lighter cream at the centre.

practice.q: **Dyes in ink** can be separated by —
practice.solution: In **chromatography** the dye parts travel different distances up the paper because they dissolve and stick differently — used to separate dyes, pigments and drugs.

practice.q: A **mixture of salt and camphor** is separated by —
practice.solution: Camphor **sublimes** on heating and its vapour condenses on a cold surface, leaving salt behind.

practice.q: **Milk** is an example of —
practice.solution: Milk is liquid fat droplets dispersed in water — an **emulsion** (liquid in liquid). Fog is an aerosol; smoke is solid in gas.

practice.q: The **scattering of a beam of light** by colloidal particles is called the —
practice.solution: The **Tyndall effect** makes the beam's path visible in fog or a colloidal solution. **Brownian motion** is the zig-zag jitter of the particles themselves.

practice.q: The **plum-pudding model** of the atom was proposed by —
practice.solution: After discovering the electron, **Thomson** imagined electrons embedded in a positive sphere like plums in a pudding. Rutherford later replaced it with the nuclear model.

practice.q: The correct historical **order of atomic models** is —
practice.solution: Dalton's indivisible atoms (1803), Thomson's electron model (1897), Rutherford's nuclear model (1911), Bohr's orbits (1913).

practice.q: Atoms of the same element with **different mass numbers** are called —
practice.solution: **Isotopes** share the atomic number Z but differ in neutrons (¹H, ²H, ³H). Isobars share the mass number A instead.

practice.q: The average atomic mass of chlorine (³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl) is about **35.5** because —
options: The two isotopes occur in the ratio 3 : 1
practice.solution: ³⁵Cl is about three times as abundant as ³⁷Cl, so the weighted average works out near **35.5**.

practice.q: Calcium has atomic number **20**. The electron arrangement **2, 8, 8, 2** means its M shell holds —
practice.solution: Filling order: K = 2, L = 8, then M begins; for calcium it stops at **8** before the N shell takes the last 2. (The M shell's maximum by 2n² is 18, but the actual count here is 8.)

practice.q: How many **moles** are there in **36 g of water**? (H₂O = 18 g/mol)
practice.solution: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 36 ÷ 18 = **2 moles**.

practice.q: A gas fills **600 mL at 1 atm**. At constant temperature, the pressure needed to compress it to **400 mL** is —
practice.solution: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → 1 × 600 = P₂ × 400 → P₂ = **1.5 atm**. (0.67 atm comes from dividing the wrong way.)

practice.q: A gas occupies **300 mL at 27 °C**. Keeping the pressure constant, its volume at **127 °C** will be —
practice.solution: Charles's law needs **kelvin**: 27 °C = 300 K, 127 °C = 400 K. V₂ = 300 × 400/300 = **400 mL**. Using Celsius directly is the standard error.

practice.q: The most abundant element in the **Earth's crust** is —
practice.solution: Crust order: **O > Si > Al > Fe > Ca** (mnemonic OSAIC). Oxygen is about 46% by mass.

practice.q: The **lightest metal** is —
practice.solution: **Lithium** (group 1) is the lightest of all metals — even it floats on oil. Hydrogen is lighter still, but it is not a metal.

practice.q: Which is the only **liquid non-metal** at room temperature?
practice.solution: **Bromine** is a fuming red-brown liquid. Mercury is the liquid *metal*; chlorine is a gas; iodine is a solid.

practice.q: The metal with the **highest melting point**, used as a bulb filament, is —
practice.solution: **Tungsten (W)** melts at about 3400 °C — the highest of all metals — so a white-hot filament survives. Its symbol comes from wolfram.

practice.q: The most abundant **metal in the human body** is —
practice.solution: **Calcium** (bones and teeth) tops the body's metal list; iron is the most abundant trace metal. Oxygen is the most abundant element overall.

practice.q: The chemical symbol of **potassium** is —
practice.solution: From Latin **kalium**. P is phosphorus, Po polonium, Pt platinum.

practice.q: Which symbol comes from the Latin word **plumbum**?
practice.solution: **Plumbum** = lead (Pb) — the same root gives 'plumber'.

practice.q: The **law of octaves** was proposed by —
practice.solution: **Newlands** arranged 56 elements by mass and found every 8th element similar — like octaves in music. Döbereiner had earlier found triads.

practice.q: Mendeleev's periodic table was based on —
practice.solution: **Mendeleev** used atomic mass and even left gaps for unknown elements. The modern table (after Moseley) uses **atomic number** instead.

practice.q: The **modern periodic law** states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their —
practice.solution: **Moseley** showed atomic number (protons) — not mass — decides periodicity, fixing the anomalies of Mendeleev's table.

practice.q: The modern periodic table has —
practice.solution: **18 vertical groups, 7 horizontal periods**, with 118 elements named so far.

practice.q: On moving **left to right across a period**, atomic size —
practice.solution: Nuclear charge rises while shells stay the same, pulling electrons closer — so atoms **shrink** across a period and metallic character falls.

practice.q: The elements of **group 17** are called —
practice.solution: **Halogens** (F, Cl, Br, I) — 'salt-formers'. Group 1 alkali metals, group 18 noble gases.

practice.q: Which pair of elements belongs to the **same group** of the periodic table?
practice.solution: Li, Na and K all sit in **group 1** (alkali metals) — one outer electron each, all soft and reactive, stored under oil or kerosene.

practice.q: The chemical name of **baking soda** is —
practice.solution: Baking soda = **sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃)** — a mild, non-poisonous base used in food and as an antacid.

practice.q: **Caustic soda** is —
practice.solution: **Caustic soda** = sodium hydroxide (NaOH), made with chlorine and hydrogen by electrolysis of brine. KOH is caustic potash.

practice.q: **Plaster of Paris** is chemically —
practice.solution: Plaster of Paris is **calcium sulphate hemihydrate**, made by heating gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O); with water it sets back to hard gypsum.

practice.q: **Bleaching powder** is chemically —
practice.solution: **Ca(OCl)Cl** — calcium oxychloride — disinfects drinking water and bleaches cotton.

practice.q: The acid present in **lemon** is —
practice.solution: Lemon and orange give **citric acid**. Vinegar–acetic; tamarind–tartaric; curd–lactic.

practice.q: An **ant sting** hurts because it injects —
options: Lactic acid, which lime water neutralises
Formic acid, which baking soda neutralises
practice.solution: The sting injects **formic (methanoic) acid**; rubbing baking soda (a mild base) neutralises it. A wasp sting is alkaline — vinegar is used there instead.

practice.q: **Oxalic acid** is found in —
practice.solution: **Oxalic acid** — tomato and spinach. Curd has lactic acid; vinegar acetic; apple malic.

practice.q: **Phenolphthalein** turns —
practice.solution: Phenolphthalein is **colourless in acid and pink in base** — the classic 'Pink in Base' pair.

practice.q: The pH of **human blood** is about —
practice.solution: Blood is kept between 7.35 and 7.45 — **slightly basic**. 5.5 is the tooth-decay threshold; 9 is like milk of magnesia.

practice.q: **Tooth decay** begins when the pH of the mouth falls below about —
practice.solution: Below **pH 5.5** mouth acids (made by bacteria from sugar) start dissolving tooth enamel — the standard exam value.

practice.q: The pH of a solution changes from **4 to 2**. Its hydrogen-ion concentration —
practice.solution: Each pH unit is a **ten-fold** change in H⁺; two units means 10 × 10 = 100 times more acidic.

practice.q: **Carbon dioxide** passed through lime water turns it —
practice.solution: CO₂ reacts with dissolved Ca(OH)₂ to form insoluble **calcium carbonate** — a white milky precipitate. This is the standard test for CO₂.

practice.q: The **chlor-alkali process** (electrolysis of brine) produces —
options: Washing soda and bleaching powder only
practice.solution: Electrolysing concentrated brine gives **caustic soda at the cathode, chlorine at the anode and hydrogen** — the 'chlor-alkali' trio.

practice.q: Adding water to **quicklime (CaO)** gives —
options: Slaked lime with much heat released
practice.solution: CaO + H₂O → **Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime)** + heat — an exothermic combination used in whitewashing.

practice.q: **Permanent hardness** of water is removed by —
practice.solution: **Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O)** precipitates the Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions that cause permanent hardness. Boiling only removes temporary (bicarbonate) hardness.

practice.q: Cakes and idli batter turn **fluffy** because baking soda —
options: Releases CO₂ on heating with an acid
practice.solution: NaHCO₃ + acid (or heat) gives **CO₂ bubbles** that puff up the dough. The same reaction pressurises soda-acid fire extinguishers.

practice.q: **Oil of vitriol** is the old name for —
practice.solution: **H₂SO₄** — called oil of vitriol. Blue vitriol is CuSO₄·5H₂O, green vitriol FeSO₄·7H₂O, white vitriol ZnSO₄.

practice.q: When **blue copper sulphate crystals** are heated strongly, they —
options: Turn white as water of crystallisation is lost
practice.solution: Heating drives off the 5H₂O; the anhydrous CuSO₄ left behind is **white** — and turns blue again if moistened.

practice.q: **Bauxite** is the chief ore of —
practice.solution: **Bauxite** (Al₂O₃·2H₂O) gives aluminium; iron comes from haematite and magnetite.

practice.q: **Galena** is the principal ore of —
practice.solution: **Galena (PbS)** is lead sulphide. Cinnabar is mercury's ore; cassiterite, tin's.

practice.q: **Pitchblende** is an important ore of —
practice.solution: **Pitchblende** is uranium oxide (U₃O₈) — the Curies processed tonnes of it to find radium.

practice.q: **Brass** is an alloy of —
practice.solution: **Brass = Cu + Zn**; bronze = Cu + Sn. Both look golden, but the second metal differs.

practice.q: **Solder**, used for joining wires, is an alloy of —
practice.solution: **Solder (Pb + Sn)** has a low melting point, so it melts and flows around the joint easily.

practice.q: **Stainless steel** resists corrosion mainly because of the added —
practice.solution: Stainless steel = **iron + chromium (about 10–20%) + nickel** (+ carbon). The chromium forms a protective oxide skin.

practice.q: **Froth flotation** is used to concentrate —
practice.solution: Powdered sulphide ore is mixed with water, **pine oil** and air: the sulphide particles stick to the froth and float, the gangue sinks.

practice.q: **Calcination** involves heating —
practice.solution: **Calcination = carbonate ore, limited air** (CO₂ is driven off); **roasting = sulphide ore, excess air** (SO₂ escapes). Both leave the oxide.

practice.q: **Aluminium** is extracted from its oxide by —
options: Heating with carbon in a blast furnace
practice.solution: Aluminium is too reactive to reduce with carbon, so molten alumina is **electrolysed** (Hall–Héroult). Iron, less reactive, is reduced by carbon in the blast furnace.

practice.q: **Sodium** is stored under **kerosene** because it —
options: Reacts violently with air and moisture
practice.solution: K and Na are at the top of the reactivity series; exposed to moist air they catch fire. Kerosene keeps air and water away.

practice.q: Which metal occurs **free (native)** in nature?
practice.solution: **Gold** (and platinum) sit at the bottom of the reactivity series — too unreactive to form compounds — so they are dug up as the free metal.

practice.q: An **iron nail** dipped in copper sulphate solution —
options: Turns the solution green and gets copper deposited
practice.solution: Iron is **more reactive** than copper: Fe displaces Cu from CuSO₄, forming green FeSO₄; red-brown copper coats the nail.

practice.q: **Rusting of iron** requires —
practice.solution: Iron rusts only when **oxygen and water** are both present; rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Boiled water without air, or dry air alone, does not rust iron.

practice.q: **Galvanisation** is coating iron with a thin layer of —
practice.solution: **Zinc** coating — galvanisation — protects buckets and roofs; zinc corrodes first (sacrificial protection). Coating with tin gives a tin can instead.

practice.q: Which metal is **liquid at room temperature**?
practice.solution: **Mercury** is the only common liquid metal. Bromine is a liquid but a non-metal; gallium melts slightly above room temperature (in your palm).

practice.q: Pure gold is **24 carat**. The gold content of **22-carat** jewellery is about —
practice.solution: 22/24 = **0.916 ≈ 91.6%** gold; the rest (copper/silver) hardens it. Pure gold is too soft for daily wear.

practice.q: **CNG** used in vehicles consists mainly of —
practice.solution: Compressed Natural Gas is mostly **methane (CH₄)**. LPG is mainly butane; biogas is also methane-rich.

practice.q: A strong smell is added to **LPG** so leaks are noticed. The added substance is —
practice.solution: Butane and propane are odourless, so a trace of **ethyl mercaptan** gives LPG its characteristic smell as a safety alarm.

practice.q: The **best grade of coal**, with the highest carbon content, is —
practice.solution: Carbon content rises peat → lignite → bituminous → **anthracite** (over ~90% carbon) — the hottest, cleanest-burning coal.

practice.q: The **Haber process** is used to manufacture —
practice.solution: **Haber process**: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ over an iron catalyst — the base of all nitrogen fertilisers.

practice.q: **Nitric acid** is manufactured by the —
practice.solution: **Ostwald** oxidises ammonia to nitric acid over platinum. Contact gives sulphuric acid; Solvay gives washing soda; Haber gives ammonia.

practice.q: The catalyst used in the **Contact process** for sulphuric acid is —
practice.solution: **V₂O₅** oxidises SO₂ to SO₃ in the Contact process. Iron (Haber), platinum (Ostwald) and nickel (hydrogenation) are the other exam catalysts.

practice.q: The **first fully synthetic fibre** was —
practice.solution: **Nylon** (1935) was the first man-made fibre made entirely in a factory. Rayon is 'artificial silk' made from natural cellulose, so it is semi-synthetic.

practice.q: **Teflon**, the coating of non-stick pans, is —
practice.solution: **Teflon = PTFE** — slippery and heat-resistant, so nothing sticks. PVC makes pipes; polythene bags; bakelite switchboards.

practice.q: Natural rubber is **vulcanised** by heating it with —
practice.solution: **Vulcanisation** (Goodyear, 1839): sulphur cross-links the rubber chains, giving strength and elasticity — hence tyres.

practice.q: The **hardest natural substance** is —
practice.solution: **Diamond**, an allotrope of carbon, is hardest — every carbon is bonded to four others in a rigid network. Graphite, the other allotrope, is soft and slippery.

practice.q: Which allotrope of carbon **conducts electricity**?
practice.solution: **Graphite** has free electrons between its layers — used as electrodes. Diamond is an insulator despite being the hardest substance.

practice.q: Compounds of carbon with only **single bonds** are called —
practice.solution: **Alkanes** (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) are saturated — methane, ethane, propane. Alkenes carry a double bond, alkynes a triple bond.

practice.q: Which alcohol is **highly poisonous** and can cause blindness?
practice.solution: **Methanol (wood spirit)** damages the optic nerve — a few teaspoons cause blindness or death. Ethanol is the ordinary alcohol of drinks.

practice.q: **Vinegar** is a solution of about 5–8% —
practice.solution: Vinegar = dilute **acetic acid (CH₃COOH)**, made by fermenting ethanol. Citric acid is lemon's; formic acid is the ant sting's.

practice.q: **Hydrogenation** of vegetable oil into vanaspati ghee uses **nickel** as —
practice.solution: Ni **speeds up** the addition of hydrogen to the oil's double bonds but is not consumed — a catalyst. The oil turns solid at room temperature.

practice.q: **Minamata disease** is caused by poisoning with —
practice.solution: **Mercury** in factory waste entered fish in Minamata Bay, Japan. **Cadmium** causes itai-itai disease — the other 'Japanese disease' pair.

practice.q: **Carbon monoxide** is dangerous because it —
options: Binds haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen
practice.solution: CO attaches to haemoglobin about **200 times** more tightly than O₂, so the blood can carry less oxygen — suffocation without choking.

practice.q: The **Bhopal gas tragedy (1984)** involved the leakage of —
practice.solution: MIC gas escaped from a pesticide plant in Bhopal — the world's worst industrial disaster. London's 1952 killer smog was mainly SO₂.
